section: What should I continue working on?
text:
What should I continue working on?

Step 1: Explore and Identify Your 3-Boxes. Continue reflecting on and identifying what might fit into each of your three boxes: Box 1, Box 2, and Box 3. Consider several factors such as sectors, locations, job levels, divisions, job titles, duties, salary considerations, or any other factors that resonate with you. If you’re still in the process of figuring all of this out, that is okay. Take the time now to start reflecting on your career goals and aspirations and bring your thoughts, questions, and concerns to your Winter Career Appointment. The beginning of this quarter is the time to start this deep reflection before courses and capstones get busier. This will lead to you conducting a higher quality job search that is tailored to what you would truly like to do. For inspiration, see this example shared by a MEDS 2023 alum.
Step 2: Create Your List of Target Organizations. Next, compile a list of companies/organizations that align with your three boxes. These are the companies/organizations where you can envision applying your skills and talents in a meaningful way. Continue adding to your list as you move through the MEDS program and learn about new companies/organizations. These two actions aren’t about having it all figured out right away. However, it is about committing to starting your job search, exploring possible career paths, and reflecting on your own career goals and aspirations; no easy task! We encourage you to start thinking about this now, and please know we are here to support you every step of the way.
Step 3: Identify Contacts for Your Target Organizations. Utilize the Alumni & Student Finder, LinkedIn, and your personal professional contacts to identify a contact for each company/organization on your list. PRO TIP: If you can’t find a contact for a few organizations, ask your existing contacts if they know someone at those organizations. Often, you can fill in the blanks through your connections.
Step 4: Reach Out to Your Contacts for Guidance. Over the next few weeks, email 1-3 alumni or personal professional contacts on your list to request a brief in-person, Zoom, or phone meeting. This will help you continue to explore potential jobs and career paths, jump-start your networking, and help you develop lifelong contacts and mentors.
Step 5: Sign up for your Winter Career Appointment by Friday, January 16 at 5PM. Look out for an email from your assigned career advisor (either Dave, Amanda, or Miya) by the end of the week with instructions on how to sign up for your appointment. Please feel free to bring your questions, comments, or concerns related to your 3-Boxes to this appointment. We look forward to supporting you.

text:
Pre-workshop Prep

A. Install software / Create accounts
MEDS students should already have the following installed / created from summer session (but it’s worth double-checking!):






NoteTo follow along, you’ll need:






R & RStudio installed
Quarto installed – Quarto is now included with RStudio v2022.07.1+ i.e. no need for a separate download / install if you have the latest version of RStudio
Git installed / configured
A GitHub account & a personal access token (PAT) set

Please refer to the MEDS Installation Guide for detailed setup instructions.





B. Gather materials to add to your website’s landing page
During this session, you’ll have the opportunity to add some personal information to your website’s landing page. It’ll help to have an idea of what you might want to include (at least as a starting point – your website’s content will most certainly evolve over time). Consider the following before attending the workshop:

Have your professional headshot handy. Your Bren photo is a great option here! Save your photo to your Desktop (or somewhere you can easily find again) for now.
Consider which landing page template to use. We’ll be applying one of Quarto’s five available built-in templates when we create our website’s landing page. Take a peek at the template previews and identify which one(s) you like most (e.g. I’m currently a fan of jolla, but used trestles for a long while). Consider how you’d like to arrange your personal bio / info given the layout of your top choice template.
Draft a personal bio or tagline for your landing page. I recommend something that’s different than your Bren bio – a shorter, catchier one that’s infused with a bit more of your personality – though you may certainly consider reusing parts of your Bren bio (taglines are great here too!). Consider the tips and examples in the dropdown, below. Save your text in a place you can quickly copy from during class (e.g. your personal branding guide document!).







TipSome considerations and example website bios






Resepct your readers’ time. The average attention span of an internet user is ~8 seconds, which means you want to succintly share your most important qualities, interests, and personal facts. Keeping website bios short and to-the-point is ideal. Save longer-form bios for a different page (e.g. I have a separate “about” page where I share about myself in a bit more detail)

Here’s a nice short post on crafting a personal tagline and another with tips on writing a personal bio

Choose the right landing page template for your bio. For example, jolla works well with short bios or taglines, while trestles might be a better choice if you’re looking to add longer and / or multiple sections.
Check out a few example websites for bio inspiration. Here are just a small handful of websites, each with a slightly different approach to their landing page bios:

Nick Lyon (NCEAS Data Analyst)

Gather your important public profile links. Your personal website is an excellent place to link out to your other public profiles in one, organized place (again, your personal branding guide is a great place to keep these). Bookmark / save the links you’d like to include (e.g. LinkedIn, GitHub, even your preferred email address)

title: Creating your personal website using Quarto
section: What should I continue working on?
text:
What should I continue working on?

Revisit & seek feedback on your personal bio. Does your landing page bio fit your personal brand? Consider what information you include and your tone – does it make sense to revise your bio to better fit your brand? Consider if your chosen template suits your needs, or if a different layout might work better. Share your bio with friends, family, a Career Team member, etc. and ask for their thoughts / feedback. You should also revisit your bio regularly (at least once a year) to make sure the content is still relevant and reflects your professional and personal identity.
Consider editing or adding additional pages. Your website scaffolding includes an “about” page where you may consider adding a longer-form biography or information. You may also decide to add additional pages, as needed.
Hide any pages that aren’t “complete.” Want to include an “about” page (e.g. like mine) but don’t quite have the content sorted out yet? It’s best to hide this until you’re ready to share something that’s fairly polished. Comment out the necessary pages in _quarto.yml (see example below), then rebuild your site and push to GitHub. Note that while you can do this for almost all in-progess pages, you must keep index.qmd “live” (i.e. don’t comment it out).




_quarto.yml

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs

website:
  title: "My website title"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      # - about.qmd

# ~ additional metadata excluded for brevity ~

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Always consider web accessibility

  


Web accessibility means that websites, tools, and technologies are designed and developed so that people with disabilities can use them. More specifically, people can perceive, understand, navigate, and interact with the Web, and contribute to the Web



-W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Improve your GitHub profile page accessibility

A few simple ways to ensure that assistive technology can help users understand and navigate your README:


Make links descriptive: assistive technologies present links in isolation, so provide context

e.g. opt for “Find the EDS 296-1F course description…” rather than “Find the EDS 296-1F course description here”





Add alt text to images: screen readers read alt text descriptions out loud

e.g. in html, <img src="image-url.com" alt="This is alt text">





Use proper heading structure: helps people understand content structure and more easily navigate sections

e.g. use # for your title, then the appropriate level-header thereafter (don’t skip levels)





Structure lists with proper markup: helps people understand lists as they are intended

e.g. use * or - for each list item, rather than special characters or emojis



The above pointers come from the github.blog post, 5 tips for making your GitHub profile page accessible.
Importantly, these tips apply for all web pages, not just your GitHub profile README!

Why should you blog?

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Website vs. Blog





Quarto Website











Has a dedicated landing/home page



Quarto Blog











Features a listing page as the landing page



The good news: you can add a blog to your existing Quarto website!

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
What you need to add a blog

 

 A folder to hold your blog posts

 A listing page that displays all blog posts

 Actual blog post content

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Part I

Setting up your blog’s structure

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 1: Create a posts/ folder

Create a posts/ folder in your root directory:




Positron:
Hover over your repo name in the Explorer pane > click “New Folder…” > type posts > press Enter



RStudio:
In the Files pane, click “New Folder” > type posts > click OK

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 2: (Optional) Add _metadata.yml

A _metadata.yml file inside posts/ applies settings to all posts automatically





posts/_metadata.yml

# re-render posts only when source changes ----
freeze: auto

# banner style title blocks ----
title-block-banner: true




freeze: auto — only re-renders posts when source files change (great for computationally heavy content)
title-block-banner: true — creates a banner-style title block at the top of each post

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 3: Create a listing page

A listing page auto-generates content from your blog posts (titles, dates, categories, preview images)

Create posts.qmd in your root directory with minimal content to start:


posts.qmd

---
title: "My Blog"
---



Positron: Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P > “Quarto: New Document” > save as posts.qmd in root directory
RStudio: File > New File > Quarto Document… > save as posts.qmd

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 4: Configure your listing page

Add a listing field to your posts.qmd YAML:


posts.qmd

---
title: "My Blog"
listing:
  contents: posts    # must match your folder name from Step 1
  type: grid         # options: default, grid, or table
  sort: "date desc"  # newest posts first
  categories: true   # enables category filtering
---

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Three built-in listing page styles



See Quarto docs for a full preview of each listing type

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 5: Add your listing page to the navbar

Update _quarto.yml to include posts.qmd just like any other page:


_quarto.yml

website:
  navbar:
    title: myWebsiteTitle
    right:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - about.qmd
      - posts.qmd   # add your listing page here

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 6: Preview your site

Run quarto preview in your terminal to see your changes:
quarto preview



Your listing page will be empty until you add your first blog post — that’s expected!

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Part II

Creating your first blog post

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 1: Create a subdirectory inside posts/

Each post gets its own folder inside posts/ using this naming convention:

YYYY-MM-DD-short-post-description




The folder name becomes the URL slug for your post — keep it short and descriptive!

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 2: Create index.qmd inside your subdirectory


Name your post file index.qmd — this keeps your URLs clean:




With index.qmd ✓

yoursite.com/posts/
  2022-10-24-my-post/


With my-post.qmd ✗

yoursite.com/posts/
  2022-10-24-my-post/
  my-post.html



The index.qmd approach creates shorter, cleaner URLs that are easier to remember and share

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 3: Configure your blog post YAML



posts/2022-10-24-my-post/index.qmd

---
title: "My first blog post"
description: "A short description that appears on the listing page"
author:
  - name: Your Name
    url: https://yoursite.com/
    affiliation: Master of Environmental Data Science Program @ The Bren School
    affiliation-url: https://ucsb-meds.github.io/
date: 10-24-2022
categories: [Quarto, R, MEDS]
citation:
  url: https://yoursite.com/posts/2022-10-24-my-post/
image: preview-image.png
draft: false
---

Here is where your blog post content begins...

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Key YAML fields








Field
Purpose




title & description
Both appear on your listing page


author
Can include name, url, orcid, affiliation


date
Post date (format: MM-DD-YYYY)


categories
Self-defined tags — enables filtering on listing page


citation
Auto-generates a BibTeX citation at the bottom of your post


image
Preview image shown on listing page — file must live in the same folder


draft: true
Hides from listing page while you work — set to false to publish

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Step 4: Simplify with _metadata.yml

Move repeated author info to _metadata.yml so you only write it once:




posts/_metadata.yml

freeze: auto
title-block-banner: true

# author info applied to all posts ----
author:
  - name: Your Name
    url: https://yoursite.com/
    affiliation: MEDS @ The Bren School
    affiliation-url: https://ucsb-meds.github.io/




posts/2022-10-24-my-post/index.qmd

---
title: "My first blog post"
description: "A short description"
date: 10-24-2022
categories: [Quarto, R, MEDS]
citation:
  url: https://yoursite.com/posts/
       2022-10-24-my-post/
image: preview-image.png
draft: false
---



Author info is inherited from _metadata.yml — override it in a post’s YAML when co-authoring

Advanced Features

Footnotes, citations, and more

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Adding footnotes


Method 1 — Referenced:
I am going to insert a footnote here[^1].

[^1]: Here is the associated footnote text.

Method 2 — Inline:
I am going to insert an inline footnote here^[Here is my inline footnote].

All footnotes are automatically collected in a “Footnotes” section at the bottom of your post.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Adding citations

Step 1: Create a references.bib file inside your post folder
Step 2: Add bibliography to your post YAML:
bibliography: references.bib
Step 3: Add references in BibTeX format to your .bib file:
@online{csik2021,
  author = {Samantha Csik},
  title  = {Why Create Presentation Slides about Blogging When You Can Just Blog about It?},
  date   = {2021-09-24},
  url    = {https://samanthacsik.github.io/posts/2021-09-21-distill-blogs/},
  langid = {en}
}
Step 4: Cite in your text using [@key]:
This was explored in previous work [@csik2021].

text:
The easier way: Visual Editor citations



In Positron or RStudio: open the Visual editor > Insert > Citation — Quarto automatically updates your .bib file. No manual BibTeX formatting required!

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
LLM vocabulary


LLM
Large language model: predicts the next piece of text from patterns in its training data


Prompt
Everything you send the model: your question, pasted data, instructions


Token
The unit a model reads and writes; a word or part of a word


Context window
The maximum number of tokens the model can work with at once


System prompt
Hidden instructions the tool gives the model before your prompt


Hallucination
Confident output that is false: a made-up function, column or citation


Non-determinism
The same prompt can give different answers each time you run it


Agent
A model that can use tools (read files, run code) in a loop toward a goal



Non-determinism matters for the activity: pairs will get different outputs from the same prompt. That’s expected, and it’s another reason to verify.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
section: Tokens: how the model reads text
text:
Tokens: how the model reads text
Models don’t read words or characters. They read tokens.

Thesquirrelranuptheoaktree.


Illustrative split. The exact tokens depend on each model’s tokenizer.



Rules of thumb (English text)

One token is roughly ¾ of a word
Common words are one token; rare words, numbers and code split into several
Tools limit and bill usage in tokens


Why it matters for data work

A pasted CSV costs tokens for every value
glimpse() + 5 rows: a few hundred tokens
A full dataset can fill most of the window, leaving less room for your instructions

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
The context window
The model’s working memory for one request, measured in tokens. Everything below shares it:

System promptAttached filesChat historyYour promptResponse



What happens as it fills

The response has to fit too
Older messages may be summarized or dropped
Details buried in a long chat get less attention


What to do

Send structure, not raw data
One task per chat; start fresh when it drifts
Restate key constraints in the new chat








Note


Window sizes vary widely by model and tool, and change often. Check the docs for the one you use.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
What’s in the context window?
The model answers using only what’s in its context window for this request.


Usually in context

Your prompt and the chat so far
Files or selections your IDE assistant attaches (open editor, @-mentioned files)
Output you paste in (errors, glimpse())


Usually not in context

The actual values in your data frame
Your project’s goals, field conventions, data-collection quirks
What you decided in a different chat









Tip


Long chats drift. When the model starts forgetting constraints, start a fresh chat with a short summary of what matters.




Show where your IDE (Positron Assistant, Copilot) shows which files are attached. What gets sent varies by tool and settings, so check yours.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
What the model knows (and doesn’t)


It only knows what’s in context

It hasn’t seen your data unless you show it
Paste glimpse() output, column names, a few sample rows
Say what the data is: source, units, one row = ?


It predicts plausible text, not truth

Code that runs ≠ code that’s correct
It fills gaps with assumptions, silently
It tends to agree with your framing, even when it’s wrong









Four Tips



Give context: data, goal, audience
Be specific: tools, constraints, output format
Iterate in small steps: one task per prompt, then review
Verify: run it, check the data, ask for its assumptions





Core idea: the model’s output is only as good as the context it gets. Everything that follows is a way of supplying better context or checking the output.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
section: The model tends to agree with you
text:
The model tends to agree with you
Models are trained to be helpful, which can tip into sycophancy: following your framing even when it’s wrong (Sharma et al., 2023).


Leading prompt

“Why is fur color such a strong predictor of how squirrels react to people?”

Assumes the effect exists. You’ll likely get an explanation, not a check.

Neutral prompt

“Is there evidence in this data that fur color is related to how squirrels react to people? What would make that comparison unreliable?”

Asks for evidence and limitations.








Important


Ask questions that the data could answer “no” to.









Socratic Prompting


The neutral prompt above is an example of Socratic prompting. Instead of telling the model what to find, ask it what the evidence would need to look like.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Part 2


Prompting fundamentals





Context · specificity · iteration · verification

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Anatomy of a good prompt

Context I’m working with the 2020 NYC Park Squirrel Census in R. One row = one squirrel sighting. Columns include fur color, location, height and free-text activities.
Task Write a cleaning script for the activities column.
Constraints Use tidyverse. Don’t drop or overwrite any original values; put derived columns next to the originals.
Output One R chunk, then a list of every value you couldn’t parse.
Check Before writing code, list your assumptions and ask me about anything ambiguous.







Note


Context doesn’t have to live in every prompt. Recall from our last workshop that a system prompt or project pre prompt can carry context so you don’t have to repeat it each time.




Five parts. Not every prompt needs all five, but the first one (context) and the last one (check) are the ones people skip.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Prompting fundamentals








Fundamental
Weak prompt
Stronger prompt




Context
“Clean this data”
“This is the 2020 NYC Park Squirrel Census, one row per squirrel sighting”


Role / audience
(none)
“I’m a data manager preparing this for a public archive”


Task + constraints
“Make a plot”
“Use ggplot2, colorblind-safe palette, one plot per park”


Output format
Not specifying
“Return a single R chunk plus 3 bullet caveats”


Surface assumptions
(none)
“Before writing code, list your assumptions about each column”


Invite pushback
(none)
“If my approach is flawed, say so before writing code”










The last two rows matter most


Models fill gaps silently. Asking for assumptions and pushback is how you catch data loss before it happens.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Show the model your data (safely)
The model can’t see your data frame. Give it the structure, not the whole dataset.

dplyr::glimpse(squirrels)          # column names, types, first values
head(squirrels, 5) |> knitr::kable() # a few example rows
dput(head(squirrels, 5))           # reproducible snippet it can run



Do

Paste schema + a few rows
Describe units and how the data was collected
Mention known messiness


Don’t

Paste sensitive or restricted data into tools your institution hasn’t approved
Assume the model knows your column meanings

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Iterate in small steps

1 · Plan → 2 · Code one step → 3 · Run → 4 · Review → repeat



Instead of…

“Clean the data, fit a model and make five plots.”


Try…

“First, propose a plan in 4–6 steps. Don’t write code yet.”









Tip


Each step should be small enough that you can check it.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Verify before you trust
AI-written cleaning code can run perfectly and still lose data. Check it.

n_before <- nrow(squirrels)
clean    <- clean_squirrels(squirrels)   # AI-written function

stopifnot(nrow(clean) == n_before)       # no rows silently dropped

# how many new NAs did cleaning create in a column?
na_added <- function(before, after, col) {
  sum(is.na(after[[col]])) - sum(is.na(before[[col]]))
}

Prompts that help

“Which values does this code turn into NA?”
“Write tests that would fail if this code dropped data.”
“Explain this function line by line.”

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Does being mean help?


Dobariya & Kumar (2025), Mind Your Tone

50 multiple-choice questions (math, science, history)
Each rewritten in 5 tones → 250 prompts
Model: ChatGPT-4o




Tone
Accuracy




Very polite
~80.8%


Very rude
~84.8%



Rude prompts scored ~4 points higher.

Before you start insulting Copilot…

One model, one version, 50 questions
Multiple choice ≠ writing your analysis code
Earlier work (Yin et al., 2024) found impolite prompts often hurt performance on older models
Open question: is it rudeness, or that rude prompts are shorter and more direct?









Note


Takeaway: Tone is a variable. Directness beats deference. Hostility isn’t the skill — clarity is.




Good discussion prompt: how would you design a study to separate “rude” from “concise”? This is a reproducibility lesson too: a single-model, single-run result is a hypothesis, not a rule.

Part 3


Same data, three roles





The 2020 NYC Park Squirrel Census

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
section: Meet the data: NYC park squirrels
text:
Meet the data: NYC park squirrels


72 volunteer “Squirrel Sighters”


433 squirrel sightings


24 parks in Manhattan and Brooklyn



2020 Park Squirrel Census: counted on a single afternoon in early March 2020
Two linked tables: one row per squirrel sighting, one row per park (conditions, litter, other animals)
Records fur color, location, height above ground, activities and reactions to humans
Real-world messy: free-text notes, inconsistent heights, values like “‘Cool’ - Hank”


Source: The Squirrel Census / NYC Open Data, 2020 Park Squirrel Census

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Same data, three roles
2020 Park Squirrel Census (433 sightings, 24 parks) · “I am [role]. Clean this dataset for me.”
Different roles yielded different methods to to clean the data.
The four methods used were:



Preserved: script left the data intact without removing anything
Transformed: values were simplified or normalized, but original meaning kept



Interpreted: data changed shape (e.g. one column split into many), steering it toward a specific analysis
Discarded: values present in the raw data were silently dropped

Advance three times: data manager, then data science student, then environmental researcher. Same prompt, same data. The role decided what survived.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
What the squirrels taught us


What happened

Same prompt, same data → three different datasets
Each role’s choices were reasonable for that role
The worst losses were silent: values became NA with no warning


How to prevent it

State your goal and what must be preserved
Ask for a list of every value that was changed or dropped
Compare row counts and NA counts before and after
Keep original columns; add derived ones beside them

text:
Activity: Prompt makeover
Goal: turn a weak prompt into a strong one, and measure the difference.
Task: create a numeric height column from the squirrel census’s messy height values (ranges like ‘6–18’, free text, blanks).


Round 1 · 3 min
Weak prompt
Baseline: see what you get


Round 2 · 5 min
Add context + constraints
Objective 1: write a complete prompt


Round 3 · 5 min
Assumptions first
Objective 2: make the model show its assumptions


Round 4 · 5 min
Verify
Objective 3: check the code against the data


Pairs · ~20 minutes · start a fresh chat for each round · use claude.ai in your browser or the Claude desktop app

Pairs: one person types, one keeps score. Fresh chat each round so earlier rounds don’t leak context. Download activity-starter.R before starting.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Verify: the check function
In activity-starter.R, and worth keeping for any AI-written cleaning code:

check_cleaning <- function(before, after, col) {
  if (!col %in% names(after)) stop("Column '", col, "' was renamed or dropped")
  tibble::tibble(
    rows_before   = nrow(before),
    rows_after    = nrow(after),
    na_before     = sum(is.na(before[[col]])),
    na_after      = sum(is.na(after[[col]])),
    values_before = dplyr::n_distinct(before[[col]]),
    values_after  = dplyr::n_distinct(after[[col]])
  )
}







Tip


If na_after > na_before, the code turned real observations into missing data. Did the model warn you?

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Part 4


From prompts to agents





Write it down once: agentic coding and skills

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
section: You just did the same work four times
text:
You just did the same work four times
In the activity, every round you:



pasted the same glimpse() output
retyped “keep the original column”
copied code from chat into R
ran the check yourself








Two questions



What if the assistant could run the code and the check itself?
What if you wrote your context and rules once, and it reused them every time?






That’s agentic coding (1) and skills (2).

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Chat assistant vs. coding agent



Chat assistant

You write a prompt
It suggests code
You copy, run and check it
You paste back errors

You run the loop.



Coding agent (e.g. Claude Code)

You describe the goal
It reads your files and data
It writes code, runs it, sees errors, fixes them
You review and approve changes

It runs the loop. You stay the reviewer.









Tip


An agent can act on your files, so the fundamentals matter more, not less.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Same fundamentals, new home








Fundamental
In a chat
In Claude Code




Context
Paste glimpse() every time
It reads your repo; project notes live in CLAUDE.md


Be specific
Retype constraints
Write rules once in a skill


Small steps
“Do step 1 only”
Ask for a plan first, approve it, then let it work


Surface assumptions
“List your assumptions”
Built into the skill: before writing code…


Verify
You run the check
It runs the check script; you review the diff

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
What is a skill?


A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: written instructions Claude follows for a specific kind of task.

Frontmatter: a name and a description of when to use it
Body: the steps and rules, in plain Markdown
Claude sees every skill’s description, and loads the full instructions only when a task matches
Or run one yourself: /safe-data-cleaning
Can bundle scripts, like our check function


my-project/
└── .claude/
    └── skills/
        └── safe-data-cleaning/
            ├── SKILL.md
            └── scripts/
                └── check_cleaning.R
Project skills live in .claude/skills/ and are shared through git. Personal ones go in ~/.claude/skills/.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Today’s prompts, as a skill
---
name: safe-data-cleaning
description: >
  Clean or recode a column in an environmental dataset
  without losing data. Use when asked to clean, tidy,
  recode or parse a column.
---

## Before writing code
1. Run `glimpse()` and `count()` on the target column.
2. List each kind of value and how you'll convert it.
3. Ask about anything ambiguous; wait for my answers.

## Rules
- Never overwrite or drop original columns; add new ones.
- Never drop rows. Use the tidyverse.

## After writing code
- Run `scripts/check_cleaning.R`; report rows and NAs.
- List every original value that became NA.

Rounds 2–4 of the activity, written down once. It’s in this repo at .claude/skills/safe-data-cleaning/.

title: MEDS Career & Professional Develoment
text:
Key takeaways


1 Context is everything. The model only knows what you show it.


2 Be specific. Tools, constraints, output format.


3 Go step by step. Plan first, then one task at a time.


4 Ask neutral questions. Let the data say “no.”


5 Surface assumptions. Ask what it changed or dropped.


6 Verify. Row counts, NA counts, tests. You’re the scientist.
